explanation: Fires on the token that closes or ends a document header line: comment-block terminators/continuations right after file headers (' */', '//' after the filename line in Objective-C headers), 'Circuit' in 'United States Court of Appeals, Nth Circuit', reporter suffixes like 'Cal.App.3d', and the error class name in Java exception messages (NoClassDefFoundError, NoSuchMethodError:). Weak elsewhere.

Fires inside boilerplate license/copyright headers in source files: tokens such as 'Authors', company names after 'Copyright', 'not' in 'you may not use this file', 'sell', 'WARRANTIES', the indentation before the license URL, and similar legal-header formula words (also 'APPEALS' in court headers, SQL 'You have an error'). Strongest on predictable mid-formula tokens of Apache/MIT/BSD headers; ordinary text gives little.

Fires on the token completing a fixed multi-word expression where the next word is highly predictable: 'nothing/little to [do] with', 'granted in [part]', 'relates [generally] to' in patents, 'in favor [of]', 'worry [about]', plus the comma in diff hunk headers '@@ -12[,]12'. Moderate on other collocation continuations.

Diffuse: fires on tokens in repetitive list-like or enumerative structures, notably 'import'/'java'/'android'/'com' at the start of successive Java import lines, the quote in 'ONE: "one"', commas in parameter lists, and assorted mid-sentence content words in scientific prose. No clear single trigger.

Fires on verbs/word pieces describing something ceasing, going away, or being switched off: 'goes', 'turning'/'turn ... off', 'shut down', 'gave it up', 'thrown out', 'disbanded', 'subsided', 'DISclaimed', 'absence', 'let it go'. Strength depends on the context implying disappearance/termination.

Fires on the separator punctuation inside numeric time and timestamp expressions, chiefly the colon between hours and minutes ('10:30', '03:13 PM', '2009-03-26 15:46') and the decimal point in fractional seconds or values; also colon after event names like 'UFC 158:'. Other digits/separators (version numbers, decimals) give moderate activation.

Fires on connective tokens joining two quantities or items in a compound expression, especially the 'x' in dimensions ('8 x 10', '18x24'), 'versus', '+/-', '**' exponent, '+' in time zone offsets or 'LGPLv3+', and 'with'/'and later' in license-combination phrases. Moderate on other binary operators/joiners.

Fires on a token in the middle of a compound name or number that continues a prior part: decimal points in numbers ('10.4', '82.6'), hyphens in chemical/compound names ('HLA-DRB3', 'COX-2', 'Philipps-Universität'), and connective words inside multi-word organization/proper names ('National Association for the', 'Campaign for Real Ale', 'electric and electronic'). Fires mid-unit where the expression is not yet complete.

No coherent trigger: fires on prepositions in search-methodology phrases ('searches of', 'until November 2011 for'), on subword pieces inside names and non-English words (Czech, French, Spanish, Japanese), and assorted verbs. Appears to be a mixture, with a lean toward subword tokens in non-English or proper-name text.

Fires on the token immediately before a large quantity/statistic is stated: the space or '$' before a number, and approximators like 'roughly', 'close to', 'about', 'estimated at', 'increased by', 'worth', 'half a' in sentences reporting figures. Strongest when context sets up an economic or statistical magnitude.

Fires on 'food' (esp. 'Food' in 'Food and Drug Administration', food industry/manufacturing) and related science/industry domain prefixes like 'Bio-', 'bio(analytical)', 'Technological' in university names, 'technology'. Strongest for 'Food' as a sector/organization word.

Mixture: fires on the first byte of split multibyte characters in CJK/Greek/emoji text, plus assorted subword or rare-word completions ('promisify', 'retrospect', 'adversity', 'theorists', '-ists'), and long comment dash separators. No single concept.

No clear pattern: activations spread across code tokens ('.append', 'dydt', 'Module'), subword pieces in chemistry/biology terms, and ordinary function words in prose. Cannot identify a consistent trigger.

Fires on a noun that is the possessed/attached object of a person or device, typically after a possessive or article: 'account' ('already have an account', 'your account'), 'beam' ('electron beam', 'laser beam'), 'eyes', 'name', 'voice', 'stories', 'gaze'. Strongest on 'account' and 'beam'; other possessed body/identity nouns moderate.
